coursesExamined.name: Personal & Professional Development
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

coursesExamined.name: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Examines AI's business, economic and societal implications without requiring a technical background. AI foundations and limitations lead into applications across enterprise functions and industries, labour-market change, productivity, innovation, market structure and inequality. Governance, corporate responsibility, regulation and future scenarios connect technological developments to institutional choices. Students analyze business cases and competing scholarly arguments, then investigate a country's AI readiness, workforce, regulation and industrial policy.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: This course includes a multi-faceted exploration of AI’s business, managerial, economic and related societal implications. Designed for students with a strong interest in AI, it requires no prior technical background.

coursesExamined.name: Introduction to Economics
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces microeconomic principles and short-run macroeconomic analysis. The microeconomic component examines supply and demand, strategic interaction, consumer choice, production, costs and competitive markets. The macroeconomic component introduces output, unemployment and inflation, then relates goods and financial markets through the IS-LM model. Students use algebra and graphs to explain economic behaviour and apply models to economic issues.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.

coursesExamined.name: Microeconomics & Behavior
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Develops microeconomic theory through consumer behaviour, imperfectly competitive markets and economy-wide allocation. Students examine choice under uncertainty, non-egoistic preferences and cognitive limitations, then monopoly, strategic behaviour and labour and capital markets. General equilibrium, efficiency, externalities and government complete the analysis. Algebraic problem-solving and graphical analysis are connected to the interpretation and evaluation of research papers.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: Study how consumers and producers make decisions under scarcity. Explore key concepts such as rational choice, decision-making under uncertainty, and non-egoistic preferences. Analyze market structures, strategic interactions, and factor markets. Learn how markets function and examine the impact of regulation. Develop analytical tools to better understand behavior and engage with empirical research.
coursesExamined.contribution: examines consumer and producer choice, uncertainty, market structure, externalities, regulation and empirical economic research

coursesExamined.name: Public Economics
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Examines government intervention through the efficiency and equity effects of public policy. Market failure, public goods and externalities provide foundations for studying public production, collective choice, spending and taxation. Health, education, welfare and social insurance illustrate expenditure and redistribution questions. Students apply economic models, interpret data and graphs, evaluate research and develop a research proposal and paper.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.

coursesExamined.name: Native American Histories
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Studies Native American social and cultural histories from the nineteenth century to the present through Indigenous perspectives and collaborative inquiry. Boarding schools, institutional violence, family separation and intergenerational trauma are connected to contemporary resistance, resurgence, food sovereignty and cultural expression. Storytelling, relational accountability and reciprocity inform work with Indigenous peers and knowledge holders. Arts-based collaborations and a public-history project develop respectful, accessible accounts of historical and contemporary issues.
coursesExamined.officialDescriptionRead: This course introduces students to Native American history and life from the 19th through the 21st century.  It argues that power, fear, misogyny, education, genocide, and resilience shape the Indigenous past and present. Topics we explore include the “Stolen Lives” of Indian children forcibly taken from their homes and placed in Indian Boarding Schools from the 1830’s through the 1990’s; Murdered and Missing Indigenous Women and Girls in the twenty-first century; and the individual and community forms of cultural resistance and environmental regeneration that connect past with present and future generations. We learn from the Native American scholars and 2Spirit youth that speak to and with the class. Exchange of cultural and intellectual knowledge also happens when we work with Lakota students to address contemporary challenges. Legislation, memoir, novels, and Indigenous children’s stories are central to our studies. So are the analyses of contemporary music and artistic expressions and exhibitions, as well as Hollywood and Indigenous film featuring Native American histories and lives.

academicJudgment: Retain three substantial responses to interdisciplinary arts and cultural-sector study. The closest sustains art history, heritage, museum inquiry, literature and media with actual sociology, economic models, organisations, marketing and research methods. Its complementary business courses do not become cultural economics, policy or placement. The society programme instead has actual historical-source research, Indigenous collaboration, gender/public history, art/heritage analysis, social theory and collective-action inquiry; law, ethics and EU policymaking support specific institutional questions, without cultural-policy equivalence. The media programme sustains film/media history, representation, narrative adaptation, documentary, rhetorical/creative production and environmental communication, with audience/customer research and digital institutions as complementary study. These directly engage cultural works and production/representation,not merely generic social-science coherence. The new actual US-history emphasis in FromTVtoTikTok still supports cultural identity/media enquiry,not generic platform economics. Topic-specific AI/ethics/history claims narrowed to actual evidence. Arts-health is separately owned by candidate1098 and excluded at maximum3,not claimed covered or impossible. Explicit specialist sociology/economics/policy,workshop,field-placement and empirical BA-thesis gaps remain. Independent course papers/projects receive full weight without automatically becoming the complete empirical graduation trajectory.
qualitativeDistinctness: The completed curriculum combines art history and heritage with sociology, economics, organisations, marketing, public policy, media, literature and mixed research methods. The label states that broad interdisciplinary composition rather than implying a specialist arts-management or art-history major.

Compared with the closest programme, this route removes business, organisational leadership, marketing, market research, advanced microeconomics, media archaeology, race/media, literature foundations, art-historical writing and the Renaissance Mediterranean case. It adds law, human rights, philosophy, ethics, EU politics, peace and conflict, environmental justice and a four-course History strand. Thirteen courses are shared and eleven differ. The organising choice moves from a broad arts-and-cultural-sector curriculum to culture's relationship with institutions, collective life, conflict, inequality and public challenges.

Compared with the closest programme, this route removes economics, art history, archaeology, African heritage, museums, literature foundations, organisational psychology, art-historical writing and the Renaissance Mediterranean case. It adds digital transformation, the AI economy, AI ethics, data science, advanced communication, platform media, environmental media, documentary and film-text study. Twelve courses are shared and twelve differ. Only six courses are shared with the culture-and-society route. Its organising choice is how media technologies, representation, audiences and digital change shape cultural life.

alignmentsRead: Both provide a chronological foundation in Western art and culture; UCR concentrates on visual art and does not cover literature, architecture and music to the same extent.

The direct overlap is the institutional and ethical treatment of cultural heritage: colonial collection, museum acquisition and contested ownership/repatriation. UCR studies these through African art rather than the full heritage-studies field.

Both introduce sociological concepts and perspectives for understanding social life; IBACS applies sociology specifically to arts and culture. UCR supplies a general sociological foundation, not that specialist sequence.
Both critically examine modernity, social theory and ideas of progress; UCR gives additional attention to imperialism and colonial responses.
Both introduce microeconomic and macroeconomic concepts; the comparator applies them directly to cultural and creative markets.
Both analyse choices by producers and consumers, market structure and economic evidence; the comparator is specifically cultural economics.

The partial overlap is organisational behaviour: motivation, leadership, groups, structure and culture. UCR does not establish the comparator’s specialist cultural-sector production, consumption or financing content.
Both examine audiences, engagement and marketing strategy; UCR teaches general responsible marketing rather than arts marketing alone.
Both assess technological change, innovation, risks and future strategies; UCR approaches these through responsible digital transformation across organisations.

The partial overlap is the analysis of cultural forms and representation through film. UCR primarily teaches film history, form and interpretation, with a shorter introduction to wider media; it does not reproduce the comparator’s full arts-and-media scope.
Both introduce social-science research design and evaluation; UCR also includes experimental and survey methods with descriptive and inferential statistics.

The direct partial overlap is organising, analysing and presenting quantitative data, including visualisation. UCR Data Science provides hands-on data analysis and a research project; it does not establish the full descriptive-statistics or SPSS syllabus of the external course.
Both teach hands-on qualitative design, data collection, interpretation and reflexive social research.
Both develop critical reading, writing, presentation and academic practice; UCR additionally foregrounds personal, ethical and professional development.
